Bayesian models in table_regression()

Source: R/table_regression_bayesian.R
table_regression_bayesian.Rd

table_regression() reads the stanreg fits of rstanarm and the brmsfit fits of brms::brm(), and summarizes them from their posterior draws: the posterior median, the posterior MAD SD and a credible interval. The table has no p-value and no t-statistic. The probability of direction is an opt-in column, and every table is backed by a check of the sampler diagnostics. Multilevel fits report their random effects as a block of rows, summarized from the draws.

Usage

table_regression(
  models,
  ci_method = c("wald", "profile", "boot_percentile", "hdi"),
  standardized = c("none", "refit", "posthoc", "basic", "smart", "pseudo"),
  exponentiate = FALSE,
  show_columns = NULL,
  ...  # the arguments of every class: see ?table_regression
)

This family has no argument of its own. The other arguments are documented in table_regression(); the values they take for Bayesian models are listed below.

Engines

ClassEngineAMEExponentiateBlocksvcov
stanregrstanarm::stan_glm(), rstanarm::stan_glmer()yes (draws)link-dependentRandom effects (if multilevel)classical (the posterior)
brmsfitbrms::brm()yes (draws)link-dependentRandom effects (if multilevel)classical (the posterior)

AME: whether the average-marginal-effects columns are available; yes (draws) means the effect is computed per posterior draw. Exponentiate: what exponentiate = TRUE gives. Blocks: the labeled blocks of rows the class adds below its coefficients. vcov: the values of vcov the class accepts. The same rows are returned by subset(table_regression_models(), family == "Bayesian").

What the table shows

Coefficient rows. B is the posterior median, SE the posterior MAD SD, and the interval an equal-tailed credible interval (header 95% CrI). See Posterior summaries and intervals.

Random-effects rows. Multilevel fits (stan_glmer, brm with grouping terms) report their random effects as a block: the posterior median SD and credible interval of each component, from the draws, with no likelihood-ratio line in the note.

AME. Draws-native: marginaleffects::avg_slopes() computes the marginal effects per posterior draw, and the table reports their posterior median, MAD SD and credible interval (equal-tailed or HDI, as ci_method says).

Fit statistics. By default, n and the Bayesian R-squared; see Fit statistics.

Values of the shared arguments

ci_method

The default gives the equal-tailed credible interval. "hdi" (Bayesian fits only) gives the highest-density interval instead, the shortest interval that holds ci_level of the posterior draws (Kruschke 2015), with the header 95% HDI. Unlike the equal-tailed interval the HDI is not transformation-invariant, so under exponentiate = TRUE it is recomputed on the exponentiated draws rather than transformed. "profile" and "boot_percentile" are refused: a posterior has no profile likelihood and no bootstrap replicates.

standardized

"posthoc", "basic" and "smart", for fixed-effects fits: stan_glm-style stanreg models and standard-formula brm() models, whose design matrix is recovered through insight. They are exact affine rescales of the link-scale summaries: the median, MAD SD and credible bounds all scale by the same positive SD ratio, and the beta stays on the link scale under exponentiate = TRUE. The Gaussian family divides by SD(y); every other family standardizes the predictors only, the frequentist glm convention. The scale factors do not depend on the engine, so the same model fitted with rstanarm or brms gets the same betas up to sampling noise. See What is refused, and why for the other cases.

exponentiate

All quantities are computed from the exponentiated draws directly: the SE is the posterior MAD SD on the ratio scale, not a delta-method approximation.

show_columns

The group presets ("all_b", ...) expand without the p-value and t columns. "pd" adds the probability of direction (Makowski et al. 2019), defined in the note. "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail" and "mcse" add per-coefficient diagnostics in an all-Bayesian table; see Diagnostics. "p" and "ame_p" have nothing to fill: refused as atomic tokens, dashed in a table that mixes Bayesian and other fits.

show_fit_stats

"r2_bayes", "elpd_loo", "looic" and "waic". See Fit statistics.

vcov, cluster

"classical" only: the displayed uncertainty comes from the posterior draws. Model the clustering with group-level terms instead.

Posterior summaries and intervals

B is the posterior median and SE the posterior MAD SD, the scaled median absolute deviation: the pairing of Gelman, Hill & Vehtari (2020) and of rstanarm's own print, equal to the posterior SD for a normal posterior. The interval is an equal-tailed credible interval (95% CrI), or the highest-density interval under ci_method = "hdi" (95% HDI). There is no p-value and no t-statistic, and so no stars and no p_adjust. The probability of direction, "pd", is the opt-in posterior summary closest to them.

The AME and the standardized betas follow the same logic: each is summarized from its draws, by the median, the MAD SD and the credible interval of ci_method.

Diagnostics

Every table is backed by an automatic check of the sampler: R-hat >= 1.01, ESS below 100 per chain, floored at 400 so that fewer chains never weaken the bar, divergent transitions, E-BFMI < 0.2. The R-hat and ESS bars of 1.01 and 400 are those of Vehtari et al. (2021, pp. 671-672). A problem adds a line to the note and raises a warning of class spicy_bayes_diagnostics, nested under spicy_caveat, so withCallingHandlers(spicy_bayes_diagnostics = ...) mutes the check alone. A clean fit prints nothing.

The columns "rhat", "ess_bulk" and "ess_tail" report the diagnostics of each coefficient in an all-Bayesian table, as does "mcse": the Monte Carlo standard error of the displayed posterior median. It tells how many digits a table can show: a displayed digit is Monte-Carlo stable when twice the MCSE stays below it (Gelman, Vehtari & McElreath 2026, Section 11.6). Under exponentiate = TRUE the MCSE is recomputed on the exponentiated draws.

Only MCMC fits are read: a fit with algorithm = "meanfield" or "optimizing" is refused; refit with algorithm = "sampling".

Fit statistics

  • "r2_bayes": the posterior-median Bayesian R-squared (Gelman et al. 2019), shown by default with n.

  • "elpd_loo" and "looic": the PSIS-LOO expected log predictive density and its deviance-scale twin (Vehtari et al. 2017), on request, a few seconds per model. The note gives the standard error.

  • "waic": the Watanabe-Akaike criterion, on request; PSIS-LOO is generally preferred.

An unreliable estimate adds a caveat to the note instead of being silenced: a PSIS-LOO Pareto k above the sample-size-specific threshold \(\min(1 - 1/\log_{10} S, 0.7)\) of Vehtari et al. 2024, the bound loo::loo() prints, or a WAIC p_waic above 0.4. Compare models with loo::loo_compare() outside the table.

What is refused, and why

Each refusal is a classed error.

  • Likelihood-based fit statistics ("aic", the pseudo-R-squared rows, ...): a posterior has no likelihood-based information criterion.

  • p_adjust, and the "p" column: there are no p-values.

  • A robust or cluster vcov: a posterior has no sandwich analog. Model the clustering or the heteroskedasticity instead (rstanarm::stan_glmer(), brms group-level or distributional terms).

  • ci_method = "profile" and "boot_percentile".

  • nested = TRUE.

  • standardized = "refit", which would re-run the sampler, and "pseudo". Also refused: multilevel fits (stan_glmer, stan_lmer and brm() with group-level terms), whose beta would need an explicit decomposition of SD(y); the stanreg subclasses that are not GLMs (stan_polr, stan_betareg); and brms formulas with distributional, multivariate or special terms (mo(), s(), ...). In these cases, standardize the predictors before fitting.

  • Non-MCMC fits (see Diagnostics).

References

Gelman, A., Goodrich, B., Gabry, J. & Vehtari, A. (2019). R-squared for Bayesian regression models. The American Statistician, 73(3), 307-309.

Gelman, A., Hill, J. & Vehtari, A. (2020). Regression and other stories. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/9781139161879

Gelman, A., Vehtari, A., McElreath, R., et al. (2026). Bayesian workflow. Chapman and Hall/CRC. doi:10.1201/9781003044024

Kruschke, J.K. (2015). Doing Bayesian data analysis: A tutorial with R, JAGS, and Stan (2nd ed.). Academic Press.

Makowski, D., Ben-Shachar, M.S., Chen, S.H.A. & Lüdecke, D. (2019). Indices of effect existence and significance in the Bayesian framework. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 2767. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02767

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A. & Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing, 27(5), 1413-1432. doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., Simpson, D., Carpenter, B. & Bürkner, P.-C. (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis, 16(2), 667-718. doi:10.1214/20-BA1221

See also

table_regression() for the arguments shared by all classes; table_regression_models() for the registry of supported classes and the other families; the Bayesian regression tables article.

Examples

# rstanarm samples the posterior, which takes a few seconds. The
# example runs in an interactive session only, so that the package
# checks never run a sampler.
if (interactive() && requireNamespace("rstanarm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit <- rstanarm::stan_glm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars,
                            refresh = 0, seed = 1)
  print(table_regression(fit))

  # Highest-density intervals and the probability of direction.
  print(table_regression(fit, ci_method = "hdi",
                         show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci", "pd")))
}
